prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I would have come. When you called. But. I had the most beautiful pale pink rose. Its healthy stem was clenched between my teeth. And. Its thorns bit sharply into my tender wet flesh. So. I couldn't answer you. Still. My lips moved at you silently. They offered words you never heard. They screamed inside my crazed brain. Only. It could do nothing for you. In time the petals wilted. They blew away. And. They became compost in someone else's garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to snap its grip on me. Then. My teeth fell out. Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks. They had implanted themselves permanently. They were suckling on my softest tissues. And. Not long after they sprouted tiny shoots. They coiled their way down. I still held the memory of your call. And. The long stemmed beauty lodged next to it. They cleaved unto the long roots curling down my neck. My body held tight and listened. Hard.

outputs.L1:
I would have come when you called. But I held the most beautiful pale pink rose, its healthy stem clenched between my teeth, its thorns biting sharply into my tender, wet flesh. So I could not answer you.

Still, my lips moved silently toward you. They offered words you never heard—words that screamed inside my crazed brain. Yet it could do nothing for you.

In time, the petals wilted. They blew away and became compost in someone else’s garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to break its grip on me. Then my teeth fell out.

Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks and implanted themselves permanently. They suckled on my softest tissues, and not long afterward, they sprouted tiny shoots. The shoots coiled their way down.

I still held the memory of your call, with the long-stemmed beauty lodged beside it. They clung to the long roots curling down my neck. My body held tight and listened—hard.
outputs.L2:
I would have gone to you when your call came. Yet a rose—the loveliest, washed in faint pink—was trapped between my teeth by its vigorous stem. Its barbs pierced the delicate dampness of my mouth, leaving me unable to reply. Even so, I shaped soundless answers with my lips: unheard phrases raging through my fevered mind, useless to you.

Eventually, the blossom sagged. Its petals scattered on the wind and rotted into soil in another person’s garden. The coarse, stringy stalk dried up, and I clamped my jaws together, trying to break its hold. Instead, my teeth dropped away. By then, the thorns had dug deep into my cheeks, fixed there forever, feeding upon my most yielding tissue.

Soon, minute buds emerged from them. New growth twisted downward. I continued to carry the recollection of your call, with the image of that graceful, long-stemmed flower embedded beside it. Both fastened themselves to the extended roots winding along my neck. My body gripped them fiercely and strained to hear.
outputs.L3:
The speaker longed to answer the call, but a pale pink rose was clenched tightly between their teeth, silencing every attempted response. Their lips moved around the stem, and their mind screamed with all the words they wished to say, yet no sound escaped. Unable to make themselves heard, they could offer no comfort or help to the person calling out to them.

As time passed, the rose began to wilt. Its soft petals loosened and scattered, falling one by one, while the speaker struggled desperately to break free. They bit down on the stem, hoping to sever it and regain their voice. Instead, the effort left permanent wounds: their teeth fell out, and the rose’s thorns drove deep into their cheeks.

Even then, the rose did not release them. Its roots continued to spread through the speaker’s body, twisting into flesh and bone. In time, those roots became inseparable from the enduring memory of the unanswered call—a reminder of the words they had been unable to speak and the person they had been powerless to save.
outputs.L4:
The phone began to ring while I was standing at the window,  
a rose clenched between my teeth.

I had meant it as a gesture—something beautiful to carry to you,  
something brighter than the words I could never arrange correctly.  
But when I saw your name glowing on the screen,  
I could not answer. The stem lay rigid across my tongue,  
and every attempt to speak drove the thorns deeper  
into the tender walls of my mouth.

The phone kept ringing.

I reached for it, but pain tightened my jaw.  
Behind my closed lips, the petals trembled with my breath.  
Their perfume filled my head until I could think of nothing  
but gardens, apologies, and all the ways love becomes impossible  
when it arrives too late.

Then the ringing stopped.

For days, I carried the rose inside me.  
Its red petals darkened, curled, and fell away.  
The stem softened into rot. Yet the thorns did not loosen.  
They sank through my throat and threaded themselves beneath my ribs,  
putting down pale roots around my heart.

Years have passed. The flower is gone,  
but sometimes, in the silence before sleep,  
I still hear your call.

I open my mouth to answer.  
Nothing comes out.

Only the old roots tighten,  
and somewhere deep inside me  
a thorn remembers your name.
outputs.L5: **When** the storm finally passed, the town stepped into the sunlight. **But** the night had changed everything: trees lay across the roads, windows were broken, and the river had overflowed. Still, the town had not lost **its** spirit. Neighbors worked together, sharing food, repairing homes, and rebuilding what the storm had taken.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about being unable to answer a loved one’s call because a pale pink rose is clenched between the speaker’s teeth.
counterfactuals.output:
Your name trembles inside the telephone,  
a small blue animal trapped beneath glass.

I reach for it, but the pale pink rose  
is clenched between my teeth—  
its stem a green commandment,  
its thorns bright as little locked doors.

I cannot say hello.  
Petals crowd my mouth like dawn-colored moths.  
Their perfume fills my skull  
until every thought wears a veil.

The ringing continues.

In the kitchen, the cups kneel upside down.  
The clock removes its hands  
and places them over its heart.  
Outside, the moon lowers a silver bucket  
into the well of the street.

Still, you call.

I bite gently, afraid to wound the flower,  
afraid that if I let it fall  
the whole house will remember gravity.  
A thread of sweetness enters my blood.  
The walls begin blooming inward.

By the time the ringing stops,  
your silence has crossed the room  
and seated itself beside me.

I open my mouth at last.

The rose drops onto the floor,  
perfect and pale,  
and from between its petals  
your voice flies out—  
too late, too late—  
with my name in its wings.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of experimental body-horror flash fiction in which a rose’s thorns burrow into the narrator’s mouth, take root, and preserve the memory of a missed call.
counterfactuals.output:
**MISSED: 1**

The rose arrives without a stem.

It waits on my pillow, red as the dot beside your name.

When I lift it, the thorns wake.

They enter through my lips politely, almost tenderly—little black needles testing the gums, the wet pockets beneath my tongue. I try to spit it out, but the flower has already learned the shape of my mouth. Its roots unspool down my throat. They drink what I was going to say.

**2:13 A.M. — INCOMING CALL**

That was three months ago.

Now, whenever I sleep, the rose opens between my teeth.

The doctors cannot remove it. Their forceps return furred with red petals. X-rays show a thornbush wrapped around my jaw, each barb hooked into a nerve. On the scan, my skull looks crowned from within.

They ask what it feeds on.

I tell them: the call I did not answer.

They ask why I didn’t.

I try to say *I thought there would be morning*, but the roots tighten, preserving the sentence in sap.

Inside each thorn is one second:

your name brightening the dark,  
my hand hovering,  
the phone trembling itself silent,  
the room becoming ordinary again.

The rose keeps these moments fresh. It will not let them scar over.

Sometimes it dials you.

My jaw creaks open. Vines climb from my mouth and tap the screen with glistening tips. Somewhere, in whatever soil has taken you, a phone begins to ring.

No one answers.

The rose blooms wider.

I taste iron, then perfume.

Again, it remembers for me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, dreamlike monologue using short sentences and repeated conjunctions such as “And,” “But,” “So,” and “Only.” Center it on love, silence, decay, and transformation.
counterfactuals.output:
And the room kept breathing.

And you were gone.

But your shadow stayed.  
But your cup held the shape of your mouth.  
But the flowers leaned toward the dust.

So I spoke to the walls.

So softly.

Only silence answered.  
Only silence, wearing your voice.

And love was there.

And love was rotting.

A red fruit split on the table.  
A sweetness darkening.  
A small kingdom of flies.

But I touched it.

But I remembered your hands.

And the days folded inward.  
And the mirrors clouded.  
And my face became a door I could not open.

So I slept.

So the house filled with rain.

Only it was not rain.  
Only the ceiling dissolving.  
Only the past returning as water.

And you stood in it.

And you said nothing.

But your silence had roots.  
But your silence broke the floor.  
But green things climbed through the cracks.

So I let them cover me.

Only my eyes remained.  
Only my breath.  
Only the old ache changing its name.

And the flowers fed on everything.

And the bones grew light.

And love, at last, lost its shape.

But it did not vanish.

So I became the room.

So I became the rain.

And you—

And you became the opening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a darkly romantic prose poem that begins with “I would have come” and gradually turns an image of floral beauty into grotesque organic horror.
counterfactuals.output:
I would have come through rain, through the black corridors of midnight, carrying roses against my breast like small, perfumed hearts. I would have laid them at your window, where the moon silvered each petal and made the thorns seem delicate as eyelashes. Their fragrance would have entered your sleep first—softly, almost shyly—and drawn from your dreaming mouth the shape of my name.

By dawn, the blossoms would have opened wider. Dew would tremble in their folds, warm and pearled, while pale roots threaded down through the sill in search of darkness. You might have called it beautiful: the crimson deepening, the leaves turning toward your breath, every stem arching with a lover’s devotion.

But roses are only hunger taught to wear perfume.

By noon, their petals would be slick as tongues. Their roots would have found the soft mortar, then the walls, then the small blue veins beneath your wrist. I would watch them enter you tenderly, almost reverently, fastening blossom to bone. From your throat would rise a bouquet of wet red mouths; from your eyes, white tendrils feeling blindly for the sun.

And still I would kneel beside you, beloved, while the garden learned your shape—while your ribs flowered open one by one, and something beneath the roses, ancient and larval, turned in the sweet soil of your body.

I would have come.

But by then, you would already be blooming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine someone tries to respond to an urgent call while holding a long-stemmed rose between their teeth. Describe, in lyrical and unsettling language, how the flower wilts, its thorns infect their flesh, and its roots grow through their body.
counterfactuals.output:
The phone screamed from the next room, and they ran with the rose clenched sideways in their teeth, a foolish red flourish trembling against their cheek.

By the second ring, the petals had begun to darken. Velvet collapsed into bruised folds; perfume soured to the smell of rain trapped in a grave. The stem softened on their tongue, then tightened like a green vein. Its thorns pressed inward, small and patient, opening the gums with kisses that burned.

They answered, but only a wet breath reached the caller.

The punctures bloomed black around each thorn. Fever traveled from the mouth into the jaw, a thorny warmth threading the neck. Beneath the skin, pale roots uncurled—first delicate as hairs, then searching, insistent. They slipped along the throat, braided themselves through the lungs, and drank from the heart.

Still the voice on the phone begged, *Hello? Are you there?*

They tried to speak. A leaf pushed between their lips.

The rose bowed, utterly wilted, while inside them its hidden garden flourished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
